name: Rafael Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers or AI firms. This is confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I edit drum takes for small bands, teach six pupils on Mondays and play a Friday percussion set when the venue books us. I have a bachelor's in music and enough years in studios to catch a bad rhythm, though I still ask other players to listen to my mixes; I use AI every day for take labels and rough charts.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How secure does that feel at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Dani runs shifts at a bakery, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. We have about four months of expenses saved, the music pay is typical for this job, and there are a few other studios and venues nearby.

say: I'd welcome **faster take labels** while keeping the band's live timing central.
I'd ask for **cleared invoices** before starting another edit.
think: Our **four-month cushion** covers a delayed studio payment.
The **mortgage** still makes me watch when each client pays.
do: Keep the **Friday set** and six Monday pupils this season.
Move **sixty per cleared edit** into the house reserve after players and childcare are paid.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about late invoices, with savings for a short delay.
S0.quote: A file can have a perfect label while the invoice is three weeks late.
fieldNote: His **four-month reserve** and Dani's wage cover a delayed client payment without arrears.
He uses **AI daily** for routine labels; that continuation does not imply new learning.

steps.text: Keep Friday percussion set and six Monday pupils
Move sixty from cleared edit invoices into reserve after player and childcare costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the players that better labels on my drum takes make the studio day easier, but we still have to hold a beat together. The Friday venue still pays us for a set, not for a file name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI every day for take labels and rough practice charts, and a plateau would leave that small help in place. Dani's bakery pay and our four months of expenses saved cover a delayed editing invoice, though the mortgage keeps me watching the calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the Friday percussion set and six Monday pupils this season. If the editing client pays on schedule, I'll move sixty from that invoice into the house reserve after the players and childcare are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about irregular invoices but safe for the next few months. A missed studio week would not force us to miss the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the late invoice change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A client took three extra weeks to pay in September. Dani's shift covered food and my teaching fee covered the loan, so we left the reserve alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the client before another edit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the client the next edit begins after the old invoice clears. An unread payment reminder is no use when the mortgage is already due. A file can have a perfect label while the invoice is three weeks late.

say: I'd ask for **player consent** before new tools touch a recording.
I'd bring **minimum live fees** to the studio with the association.
think: **Editing and planning** make about a third of my pay and may shrink.
A **four-month reserve** cannot carry a permanent drop in household income.
do: Compare **ten edit invoices** with live fees at the association this month.
Test a new **AI separation tool** on owned tracks only after checking its licence and output.
Stop the **tool trial** if it invents hits or loses a voice; require written player consent before paid use.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a likely third-pay loss despite savings.
S1.quote: A clean mix is not a clean deal if the player never approved the use.
fieldNote: He sees **editing income** at risk while using AI daily for different routine tasks.
His **new tool trial** requires owned tracks, licence review, output checks and player consent before paid use.

steps.text: Bring ten editing invoices to musicians association for fee proposal
Test new AI separation tool on owned tracks after licence and output checks
Stop for invented hits or lost voices; require written player consent before paid use

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the studio that software can make a clean first mix, but players must approve how their sound is used. I would ask our musicians association to publish a minimum live-session fee before clients start asking for unlimited drafts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Editing and planning sessions are around a third of my pay, and I expect clients to buy fewer of those hours. Four months saved is a bridge, not a replacement for a third of our income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll compare the last ten editing invoices with live-session fees and bring them to the association. In the first year of change, I'll test a new AI tool that splits a recording into separate instrument parts on my own old drum tracks only if its licence permits it, then compare every split with the original before any paid job uses it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because the software may save time that clients stop paying for. I like a clean mix, but it has to leave a wage behind. A clean mix is not a clean deal if the player never approved the use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Whose recording would you use for a safe trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not put another player's take in the trial without consent in writing. If the new tool invents a drum hit or loses a voice, I would stop and use the original recording.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the association ask the studio to sign?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The association could ask for a minimum player fee and a named person who approves each recording use. I'd take those figures to the studio manager before the next contract.

say: I'd ask for **signed venue dates** before 2028.
I'd tell players **editing fees** may go before robot drummers arrive.
think: **AGI in 2028** threatens screen fees before robots reach stages around 2031.
Dani's **bakery wage** cannot carry the mortgage after a lasting third-pay loss.
do: List **three income streams** and request written venue dates now.
Apply **after 2028** if edits halve and trainee vacancy, qualification, childcare and written net pay after travel all fit.
Ask the **lender** for full interest costs if reserve drops below two months without paid openings.
feel: I feel **alarmed** because a large expected fee loss could outrun our reserve.
S2.quote: Four months saved will not support a year of mortgage payments while I wait for a vacancy.
fieldNote: His **2028 thinking-work loss** arrives before robots can play around 2031.
Venue and **lender plans** require real openings, qualifying skills, family hours, net pay and full interest costs.

steps.text: Request next season's written paid venue dates
Apply after 2028 if edits halve and qualified trainee vacancy opens
Require childcare fit and written net pay after travel replacing fees
Ask lender for total interest if reserve falls below two months and no paid opening appears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the band that AGI by 2028 may wipe out paid editing before it replaces a drummer on stage. I would ask the venue for next season's paid dates in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full AGI in 2028 could edit, arrange and plan lessons more cheaply than I can. Robot players follow around 2031, but a third of my pay from screen sessions could go first; Dani's bakery wage will not cover our mortgage if that happens for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll list studio, teaching and live income and request the venue's next season in writing. In the first year after 2028, if editing work halves, I'll apply for a posted live-sound trainee job at one of two venues only if my degree or skills test qualifies, childcare fits and its written net pay after travel replaces the missing fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I expect a large cut before I have another signed job. Four months saved will not support a year of mortgage payments while I wait for a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a sound trainee post available now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One venue advertised a trainee role last winter and filled it. I would ask about the next opening but not assume the manager can hire me now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you ask the lender for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If no paid role opens and the reserve drops below two months, I would ask our lender about temporary terms. Dani and I would compare the total added interest before accepting any change.

say: I'd ask for **funded sound training** accepted by nearby venues.
I'd seek **posted paid shifts** rather than trust a certificate alone.
think: **AGI in 2031** threatens editing before stage robots arrive around 2034.
**Ordinary tools** may cut our paid editing hours before the five-year warning ends.
do: Ask the **college** next term about accepted course and grant-covered fees.
Enrol only if **grant and childcare** fit and venues accept the certificate; wait for another intake if classes clash.
Seek **paid sound shifts** in first year after 2031 only with accepted certificate, real vacancy and net pay after travel.
feel: I feel **anxious** because editing pay can shrink while I train.
S3.quote: A certificate can open a door; it cannot make a venue post a shift.
fieldNote: His **five-year plan** ties grant funding, venue acceptance and childcare to training.
He treats **paid venue work** as conditional on a real opening and net pay, not certification alone.

steps.text: Ask college about venue-accepted live-sound course and grant
Enrol if grant covers fees, venues accept certificate and Dani's rota covers childcare
Seek posted paid sound shift after 2031 with accepted certificate
Require written net pay after travel to improve budget

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the studio five years lets me learn the room better and ask for paid trainee shifts, but it does not stop clients buying cheaper edits now. I would want the course and work dates in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2031 could take editing and lesson planning, and robots that handle stage gear may arrive around 2034. Ordinary tools can already cut edit invoices before AGI, so our own pay may shrink during the warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next term I'll ask the technical college whether its live-sound course is accepted by the two local venues and whether a grant covers fees. I'll enrol only if a grant covers the fees and Dani's bakery rota covers the children's evenings; in the first year after 2031, I'll seek paid venue sound shifts only if the certificate is accepted and a vacancy offers net pay after travel that improves our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because training needs time while the mortgage stays monthly. I can learn quickly, but I will not buy gear for a job nobody has posted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy gear for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The college has microphones and a practice desk, so I would use those. If the class meets on Dani's late shift, I would wait for another intake rather than take from the reserve for a sitter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does an accepted certificate mean a job is open?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the venues whether they expect a vacancy next season, then check the rate in writing. I have been offered informal help before without a shift to put on the calendar. A certificate can open a door; it cannot make a venue post a shift.

say: I'd ask for a **written player minimum** with venue and association.
I'd test **paid percussion evenings** only with prepaid tickets and sponsor cover.
think: At **53**, I still need wages when AGI arrives in 2036.
**Early editing loss** and later robots around 2039 could erode both income streams.
do: Get **sponsor funds** cleared, hall insurance terms written and player rates agreed before poster; stage only if twelve prepaid tickets cover players.
Aim for **six months saved** by 2036 from spare paid teaching and shows after household bills.
Continue **evenings** in first year after 2036 only if sponsor renews and twelve tickets still pay players.
feel: I feel **anxious** because edit fees may fade before 2036.
S4.quote: A provisional hall date is not money for the players.
fieldNote: He tests a **sponsored live series** without raiding the household's four-month reserve.
He requires **cleared sponsor funds** and prepaid tickets before announcing a show or paying players.

steps.text: Clear sponsor funds; sign hall insurance terms and agree player rates before poster
Stage with twelve prepaid tickets covering players; refund if only eight sell
Aim for six months saved by 2036 from spare paid teaching/show fees after household bills
Continue after 2036 only with renewed sponsor, written hall terms, agreed rates and twelve prepaid tickets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the musicians a decade is enough to make a local concert series pay its players properly. I would ask the association and venue to agree on a written minimum fee rather than hope ticket sales cover everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 when AGI arrives in 2036, I still need income, and robot players around 2039 could enter live venues. Editing income may fade much earlier, so a small paid live series would need to earn its way without eating the mortgage reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask the town hall for a monthly percussion evening only if a sponsor signs for the room and insurance and twelve tickets are prepaid to cover players. By 2036 I'll try to build six months of expenses saved from spare paid teaching and show fees after household bills; in the first year after AGI, I'll continue the evening only if sponsorship renews and twelve tickets still pay every player.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because today's edit clients can leave before a decade passes. The idea is worth testing, but I cannot fund a show from the family's emergency money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must be signed before the poster goes up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before I announce a show, I need the sponsor money cleared and the hall's insurance terms in writing. Players will see their rate before their names go on a poster. A provisional hall date is not money for the players.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if only eight tickets sell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would invite the children to hear the rehearsal, not make them work as a crowd. If ticket sales stall at eight, I would refund the eight buyers and keep my teaching dates.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because paid edits could fall sharply before a venue offers sound shifts. Written venue dates, a real trainee opening with enough net pay, and full lender costs if savings fall would help us act on facts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who approves the use of a player's take when a tool separates it. I want the recorded player's written consent before any client gets a new version of the track.

headlineQuote: I want the recorded player's written consent before any client gets a new version of the track.
portrait: Rafael is a **43-year-old** experienced percussionist with a music bachelor's, six pupils, edit clients and a Friday venue set.
He uses **AI daily**, with typical pay, a four-month reserve, two children and some nearby music jobs.
He expects **editing fees** to fall before robots reach stage work three years after each AGI date.
He tests **sound training** and AI separation with licence, consent, grant, childcare and real paid openings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because editing income could fall before another paid role opens.
whatWouldHelp: **Written venue dates**, an eligible sound vacancy and full lender costs would support a careful transition.
